About This Book

This phonics and spelling workbook belongs to Crystal Heights International School. It was prepared by the school's Phonics Team to build the foundation skills Grade 4 learners need before moving on to Grade 5 and 6. Students are now ready to “prove” words using the Five Phonetic Skills, which help them recognize likely and unlikely sequences of letters. The approach is explicit, systematic, sequential phonics taught through multi-sensory, direct instruction.

How to Use This Book

Every lesson covers 7 stages across 7 pages. A progress bar at the top of every page shows which stages are complete.

📘 Stage 1: Learn
📋 Stage 2: Word List
🗂 Stage 3: Word Sort
✍️ Stage 4: Prove It
📒 Stage 5: Working Space
📖 Stage 6: Word Meaning
🗣 Stage 7: Reading Fluency
Delivery Method
  • Have the students stand at whiteboards or chalkboards.
  • Dictate the letter, sound, or word twice to the students.
  • Use your hands to draw attention to your mouth.
  • Students repeat twice and write once on the board.
  • Students benefit from active engagement: the method uses their auditory, visual, tactile, and kinesthetic modalities.

Lesson 4: Murmur Diphthongs

A diphthong is a vowel blend. A murmur diphthong is a vowel blended with an R, so the vowel sound blends with the r sound to make a new sound: ar in car, or in fork, er in her, ir in bird, ur in turn. They are also known as r-controlled vowels.

Murmur diphthongs are predictable vowel sounds that are neither long nor short. To mark one, place an X under the vowel and arc the two letters together.

Lesson 6: Murmur Diphthong Exceptions

Some murmur diphthong words break the usual pattern. When Silent E follows directly after a murmur diphthong, the word follows Phonetic Skill 4 (fire, hire). If adjacent vowels come before a murmur diphthong, the word follows Phonetic Skill 5 (fear, air).

Whenever W, or the sound of W, comes before the vowel A or O, it changes the vowel sound (ward, work). ER and OR take the sound of short /a/ or /ar/ at the end of a word or when used as a suffix (helper, educator).

Lesson 7: Special Vowel Sounds — AU, AW, OU, OW, OI, OY

Special Vowel Sounds are diphthongs: two vowel sounds pronounced together in one syllable, as in coin, boy, house, and cow. When proving words with Special Vowel Sounds, put an X between the vowels and arc them together.

Each pair says one sound: AU and AW say /or/ (haul, saw); OU and OW say /ow/ (shout, cow), and OW can also say long O; OI and OY say /oy/ (coin, boy). AU, OU and OI come in the middle of words; AW, OW and OY come at the end.

Lesson 8: Special Vowel Sounds — OO, UE, EW, EU

The two OO Special Vowel Sounds are spelled the same but sound different: the first sounds like /oo/ in zoo, and the second like /oo/ in look.

UE, EW and EU all make the sound /ew/ (blue, few). Sometimes UE sounds like long U and follows Phonetic Skill 5. The correct spelling must be memorized. As always, put an X between the vowels and arc them together.

Lesson 14: Prefixes

A prefix is a group of letters added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning. Un- means “not” or “opposite,” re- means “again,” dis- means “remove” or “not,” and pre- means “before.”

A prefix goes at the beginning of a word; a suffix goes at the end. Prefix = before the root word. Suffix = after the root word.

Examples: happy → unhappy (not happy), do → redo (do again), agree → disagree (not agree), heat → preheat (heat beforehand), possible → impossible (not possible).

pages.name: Glossary
pages.subtitle: KEY TERMS
pages.html:
Glossary
TermMeaning
ArcA curved line drawn under letters to show they work together as one sound.
Decoding SkillA rule for finding syllable breaks: Skill 1, one consonant goes on; Skill 2, two consonants split.
DiphthongTwo vowel sounds pronounced together in one syllable (oi in coin, ou in house).
GuardianA consonant that follows a vowel and guards its sound.
Murmur DiphthongA vowel blended with r to make a new sound (ar, or, er, ir, ur); also called r-controlled.
Phonetic SkillsThe five rules used to prove a word and find the sound of its vowel.
PrefixA group of letters added to the beginning of a word (un-, re-, dis-, pre-).
ProveTo mark a word to show which phonetic rule it follows.
Root WordThe main word that remains when a prefix or suffix is taken away.
SchwaThe weak, unstressed vowel sound /uh/ heard in the _le ending.
Silent EAn e at the end of a word that is not said, but makes the vowel before it long.
Special Vowel SoundA diphthong such as au, aw, ou, ow, oi, oy, oo, ue, ew, eu.
SuffixA group of letters added to the end of a word (-ing, -ed, -er, -tion, -ous).
SyllableA word part that has one working vowel sound.
